For a given metallic wire, the potential difference across its ends is directly proportional to current provided its temperature remains the same (Ohm’s law). V is proportional to I (11.4); V/I=R is constant for the given wire at a given temperature; V=IR (11.5). Resistance R measures opposition to charge flow. R=V/I (11.6); its SI unit is ohm, with 1 ohm=1 volt/ampere. Also I=V/R (11.7). At a fixed potential difference, current is inversely proportional to resistance; doubling resistance halves current.

context.section: 11.5 Factors on which the resistance of a conductor depends
context.text: Resistance of a conductor depends on length, cross-sectional area and material. For a uniform metallic conductor, resistance is directly proportional to length l (11.8) and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A (11.9). Combining these: R=rho*l/A (11.10). The proportionality constant rho is electrical resistivity, a characteristic property of the conductor material. Its SI unit is ohm metre (ohm m).

context.section: 11.5 Factors on which the resistance of a conductor depends

context.text: If net charge Q passes through a conductor cross-section in time t, current is I=Q/t (11.1). The SI charge unit is coulomb (C); current is measured in ampere (A). One ampere means one coulomb per second: 1 A=1 C/s. 1 mA=10^(-3) A and 1 microampere=10^(-6) A.
